explanations.explanation: Judah and Jerusalem, right there in the first verse. Isaiah son of Amoz saw this vision during the reigns of four kings of Judah (Isaiah 1:1). The vision has a clear address, like a letter that actually got delivered. Everything after it is aimed there.

Good try, baker, but verse 1 doesn't name Samaria or Bethel. It says the vision concerns Judah and Jerusalem. The kings listed are kings of Judah, which is your clue. When you're unsure, check the address on the envelope.

Those are big names, but neither one shows up in verse 1. The vision concerns Judah and Jerusalem (Isaiah 1:1). It's like opening a package with somebody else's name on the label. Judah and Jerusalem is the name on this one.

That's it. The LORD says, “I have raised children and brought them up, but they have rebelled against Me.” That's a heavy verse, friend. Raising children and then getting rebellion back is the whole complaint.

explanations.answer: They asked Him for a king
explanations.explanation: Not in this verse, friend. The LORD says what His children did, and it's “…they have rebelled against Me.” Nothing here mentions a king. Stay in verse 2 and the answer is sitting right there.

Egypt isn't in this verse at all. The LORD says, “I have raised children and brought them up, but they have rebelled against Me.” Rebelling is what they did, and it's all the text says here. No travel plans in sight.

It's the other way around, friend. The ox knows its owner and the donkey its master's manger, “…but Israel does not know; My people do not understand.” The animals are the ones in the picture who know. I think that's a hard line to hear, and the LORD says it plainly.

Right, it's False. The ox knows its owner and the donkey its master's manger, “…but Israel does not know; My people do not understand.” The animals are the ones in the picture who know. It's a simple comparison, and it stings.
Yes, despised. Isaiah says, “they have despised the Holy One of Israel and turned their backs on Him.” They turned their backs on Him too. Turning your back is a quiet way to say a loud thing.
Not quite, baker. Isaiah says they “…have despised the Holy One of Israel and turned their backs on Him.” Fearing Him isn't the word he uses. Despised and turned their backs is what the verse says.

That would be a nicer verse, but it isn't this one. Isaiah says they “…have despised the Holy One of Israel and turned their backs on Him.” A thank you needs somebody facing the right direction. The text has them turned away.

It's False, friend. Isaiah says the head has a massive wound and the whole heart is afflicted. Then verse 6 says, “From the sole of your foot to the top of your head, there is no soundness…” That's head to toe, with no good spot left.

Right, it's False. Isaiah says, “Your head has a massive wound, and your whole heart is afflicted.” Then he says, “From the sole of your foot to the top of your head, there is no soundness…” He doesn't leave one healthy spot.

True. Isaiah says the wounds and welts and festering sores were “…neither cleansed nor bandaged nor soothed with oil.” That's three things nobody did. Not even a bandage, and I can find one of those in any kitchen.

It's True, friend. Isaiah says the sores were “…neither cleansed nor bandaged nor soothed with oil.” Nobody cleaned them, wrapped them or soothed them. Read the verse again and all three are right there.

Foreigners is the word. Isaiah says, “Foreigners devour your fields before you…” The verse ends with strangers having demolished the place. And the people have to watch it happen right in front of them.

Neighbors is a natural guess, but the verse uses a different word. Isaiah says, “Foreigners devour your fields before you…” The same verse also says the land was demolished by strangers. So the ones doing the devouring come from outside.

Nobles are a fair guess, but the verse points somewhere else. Isaiah says, “Foreigners devour your fields before you…” The ones doing the devouring are outsiders, and the verse calls them strangers. Those are the words to hold onto.

That's the picture. Isaiah says the Daughter of Zion “…is abandoned like a shelter in a vineyard, like a shack in a cucumber field…” Think of one lonely shack way out in a field with nobody inside. It's a picture of empty.

Close the guest list, friend. Isaiah says the Daughter of Zion “…is abandoned like a shelter in a vineyard, like a shack in a cucumber field…” The picture is abandoned, not crowded. A shack left alone in a field has plenty of room.

That's not the picture, friend. Isaiah says the Daughter of Zion “…is abandoned like a shelter in a vineyard, like a shack in a cucumber field…” The word he uses is abandoned. Think of a shack left alone in a field.

Survivors, yes. Isaiah says, “Unless the LORD of Hosts had left us a few survivors, we would have become like Sodom, we would have resembled Gomorrah.” Notice the word a few. That's a small number, and it's the whole difference.
Soldiers sound reasonable, but the verse doesn't say that. Isaiah says, “Unless the LORD of Hosts had left us a few survivors…” Survivors is the word. The verse says nothing about an army.

Prophets aren't in this verse. Isaiah says, “Unless the LORD of Hosts had left us a few survivors, we would have become like Sodom, we would have resembled Gomorrah.” The word is survivors. A few of them is the whole difference.

Rulers of Sodom is it. Isaiah says, “Hear the word of the LORD, you rulers of Sodom; listen to the instruction of our God, you people of Gomorrah!” He puts the people with Gomorrah in the same breath. He's calling out to the whole crowd.
Shepherds of Israel sounds friendlier, but it isn't in this verse. Isaiah says, “Hear the word of the LORD, you rulers of Sodom…” The label he uses is Sodom. That's a much sharper name.

That title isn't in this verse, baker. Isaiah says, “Hear the word of the LORD, you rulers of Sodom; listen to the instruction of our God, you people of Gomorrah!” Calling them rulers of Sodom is a sharp thing to say to people in charge. It's the name he picks for them, and it's not a friendly one.

It's False, friend. The LORD says, “I take no delight in the blood of bulls and lambs and goats.” He also says He is full from the burnt offerings of rams and the fat of well-fed cattle. The verse says no delight.

Right, it's False. The LORD says, “I take no delight in the blood of bulls and lambs and goats.” Before that He says He is full from the burnt offerings of rams and the fat of well-fed cattle. The sacrifices keep coming, and no delight comes with them.

That's the one. The LORD says, “Bring your worthless offerings no more; your incense is detestable to Me.” Notice the word worthless. He's talking about what they bring, so listen to what He calls it.

Gold and silver aren't named in this verse. The LORD says, “Bring your worthless offerings no more; your incense is detestable to Me.” The thing He tells them to stop bringing is the offerings. Keep your eyes on that word worthless.
No music in this verse, friend. The LORD says, “Bring your worthless offerings no more; your incense is detestable to Me.” Offerings and incense are what's named. Harps and lyres never come up.

True. The LORD says, “…I cannot endure iniquity in a solemn assembly.” Right before that He names New Moons, Sabbaths and convocations. So the gathering is the setting, and the iniquity is what He can't endure.

It's True, friend. The LORD says, “…I cannot endure iniquity in a solemn assembly.” That comes right after He names New Moons, Sabbaths and convocations. So what He can't endure is iniquity showing up in the middle of those gatherings.
Blood is the word. The LORD says, “Your hands are covered with blood.” It comes right after He says He will not listen to their many prayers. That's a heavy verse, and it's meant to be.

Dust is a fair guess for hands, but it isn't what the verse says. The LORD says, “Your hands are covered with blood.” That comes right after He says He will not listen, even though they multiply their prayers. Blood is the word.
Ashes isn't in this verse. The LORD says, “Your hands are covered with blood.” It's a hard thing to hear, and it sits right beside His words about their prayers. So blood is what He names.
Yes, their evil deeds. The LORD says, “Remove your evil deeds from My sight. Stop doing evil!” Right alongside “Wash and cleanse yourselves.” He tells them to stop. The deeds are what He wants gone.
Altars aren't mentioned in verse 16. The LORD says, “Remove your evil deeds from My sight. Stop doing evil!” What He wants removed is the evil they've been doing, and no altar comes up.

I get why you went there, since the verse does say wash. But the LORD says, “Remove your evil deeds from My sight. Stop doing evil!” The thing to remove is the deeds, and robes never come up. A clean apron is nice, but this wash goes deeper.
That's right. The LORD says, “Defend the fatherless and plead the case of the widow.” Defending and pleading are both action words. Those are the folks He names.

The king and his court aren't named in this verse. The LORD says, “Defend the fatherless and plead the case of the widow.” He points to the fatherless and the widow, not to people in high places. I think that tells us who He wants them looking out for.

Priests and Levites don't show up in this verse, friend. The LORD says, “Defend the fatherless and plead the case of the widow.” Those are the two He names, and they're the ones to stand up for. Defend and plead are things you do, not just things you feel.

It's False, friend. The LORD says, “Though your sins are like scarlet, they will be as white as snow; though they are as red as crimson, they will become like wool.” Anybody who's fought a red stain knows how stubborn red can be. That's why this promise is so big.

Right, it's False. The LORD says, “Though your sins are like scarlet, they will be as white as snow; though they are as red as crimson, they will become like wool.” Anybody who's fought a red stain knows how stubborn red can be. Scarlet and crimson are still no match for what He promises.

It's False, friend. The best of the land is promised in verse 19 to those who are willing and obedient. For those who resist and rebel, the LORD says, “…you will be devoured by the sword.” These are two very different ends.

Right, it's False. Verse 19 says the willing and obedient will eat the best of the land. But the LORD says, “…if you resist and rebel, you will be devoured by the sword.” Two choices, two ends, and the verse spells out both.
